university: The University of Texas at Arlington

documents.unit: Artificial Intelligence at UTA (Information Security, Legal Affairs, AI Steering Committee)
documents.title: Guidelines: UTA Advice on Generative AI
documents.summary: An employee-focused advisory on generative AI from Information Security, Legal Affairs and the AI Steering Committee. It welcomes staff use but restricts what data may go into public tools, and asks faculty to state allowed or limited GenAI use in each syllabus.
documents.stance_why: The only teaching-related rule is that 'faculty should state in the course syllabus any allowed or limited use of GenAI Tools within the course'; the university sets no student-use rule and hands the decision to each course, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: The page asks whether staff should use GenAI and answers with a resounding yes, which welcomes employee use by default, so P02; it addresses employees (admin/all) and is a general statement.
units.anchor: it is important to follow guidance and familiarize yourself with UTA’s policies and resources
units.policy: UTA staff should use GenAI, but first follow guidance and familiarize themselves with UTA's policies and resources.
units.fit_note: The anchor is the conditional half; the welcome itself ('a resounding Yes') spans lines in the text.

units.why: The advisory says GenAI is used by educational institutions and UTA is exploring benefits but 'must consider the inherent risks'; it is rationale for the guidance, so P87 (benefits) is nearest but the unit mainly frames risk; I chose P56 as framework preamble because it states the purpose and scope of the advisory.
units.anchor: we must consider the inherent risks of using this technology.

units.why: The advisory states its producers and its purpose, 'guidance for UTA employees on how to use GenAI Tools safely'; it sets the scope (employees, data safety) of the framework, so P56 rather than P84 because it names purpose and scope more than process.
units.anchor: guidance for UTA employees on how to use GenAI Tools safely
units.policy: The advisory gives guidance for UTA employees on how to use GenAI Tools safely, without putting personal, proprietary or university data at risk.
units.fit_note: It also names the three bodies that produced it (Information Security Office, Legal Affairs, AI Steering Committee).

units.why: The advisory is the product of named bodies, the Information Security Office, Office of Legal Affairs and AI Steering Committee; saying who made the guidance is P84 (how and by whom the policy was made).
units.anchor: Information Security Office, the Office of Legal Affairs and the AI Steering Committee

units.why: Under ALLOWABLE USE, GenAI may be used with public data; this permits use of GenAI tools conditioned on data classification, so the nearest type is P50 (protect data) with a permit stance; modality 'may'.
units.anchor: GenAI Tools may be used with data that is publicly available
units.policy: GenAI Tools may be used with data that is publicly available or defined as Public by UTA's Data Classification Standard.
units.fit_note: The unit grants a permission limited to Public data rather than only urging protection of data.

units.why: The rule that 'GenAI Tools use must be consistent with UTA's and other relevant policies' requires compliance with existing policy, which is P77.
units.anchor: GenAI Tools use must be consistent with UTA’s and other relevant policies.

units.why: The sentence tells faculty to state allowed or limited GenAI use in the syllabus, 'faculty should state in the course syllabus'; this is a syllabus-statement expectation (P09), addressed to instructors, at course start.
units.anchor: faculty should state in the course syllabus any allowed or limited use of GenAI Tools

units.why: Instructors state the allowed or limited use course by course, so the decision of what AI use is allowed is left to the faculty member, 'any allowed or limited use ... within the course'; the university sets no rule itself, so P04 (instructor sets the rule).
units.anchor: any allowed or limited use of GenAI Tools within the course
units.policy: Each course's allowed or limited GenAI use is set by the faculty member and stated in the course syllabus.

units.why: Tools installed on UTA-controlled computers or under a contract that protects university data 'may be designated as a permittable tool' for non-public data; this is an institutional approval route for tools, P65 (review and approve tools), not P92 because it is about designating approval for data classes.
units.anchor: may be designated as a permittable tool for use with non-public data classifications
units.policy: GenAI tools installed on a UTA-controlled computer or under a vendor contract that specifically protects university data and its use in the AI model may be designated as a permittable tool for use with non-public data classifications in accordance with relevant policies.

units.why: Under PROHIBITED USE, FERPA records, health and other Confidential or Controlled data 'must not be used within public AI models'; this protects personal data, P50, and is a prohibition (must-not).
units.anchor: student records subject to FERPA, health information, proprietary information
units.policy: Student records subject to FERPA, health information, proprietary information, and any other information classified as Confidential or Controlled under UTA's Data Classification Standards must not be used within public AI models.
units.fit_note: The type centers on protecting data and preferring vetted tools; this unit is the explicit ban on putting classified data in public models.

units.why: A blanket rule that GenAI cannot be used for illegal, unethical or fraudulent activity is a general conduct ban, P74 (deceptive or malicious use), not P77 because it names fraud and unethical use directly.
units.anchor: cannot be used for any activity that would be illegal, unethical, fraudulent

units.why: The Liability section says content entered into a public tool is 'available to the public' and there is 'no inherent data security and privacy protections'; it explains the risk behind the data rules, P50.
units.anchor: content entered into, or generated by, a public GenAI tool are available to the public.
units.fit_note: It is a risk statement, not a rule to protect data or use vetted tools.

units.why: The sentence states that using public AI tools 'could expose individual users and UTA to the potential loss and/or abuse of sensitive data'; this explains risk (privacy), P50, informs.
units.anchor: could expose individual users and UTA to the potential loss and/or abuse of sensitive data
units.fit_note: Risk statement rather than a protective rule.

units.why: Click-through agreements are contracts and signing without authority may carry 'personal consequences'; this is a terms-of-use warning, P52 (licensing, terms of use), informs.
units.anchor: Individuals who accept click through agreements without authority may face personal consequences
units.fit_note: Type centers on copyright and ownership of outputs; this unit is about terms-of-use contracts and personal liability.

units.why: The advisory recommends processing all GenAI tools through UTA's TAP process, i.e. institutional review before use, 'It is recommended to process all GenAI Tools through UTA's TAP process'; P65 (review and approve tools) with modality should.
units.anchor: It is recommended to process all GenAI Tools through
units.policy: It is recommended to process all GenAI Tools through UTA's TAP process to ensure appropriate use.

units.why: Readers needing more help are directed to ai.uta.edu and security concerns to the Information Security Office; this names a contact for the policy, P80 (who owns the policy), informs.
units.anchor: For security concerns, please contact the Information Security Office
units.fit_note: Names a contact for security concerns rather than an enforcing or exception-granting office.

units.why: The AI Council suggestion 'Fact Check Everything' says GenAI 'will assert its errors with great confidence' and content must be reviewed for accuracy; this is P31 (verify AI output), should, addressed to employees.
units.anchor: Review and check all AI-created content for accuracy.

units.why: Where content is beyond one's expertise, the user should seek a human with that expertise to review it; this points to human help beside AI, P72.
units.anchor: seek a human being with that expertise to review the content

units.why: Under Transparency, employees 'should consider transparently saying so' when they use GenAI, with sample statements; this is disclosure of use, P24, but with soft wording (consider), so modality should.
units.anchor: you should consider transparently saying so
units.policy: Employees who use GenAI in their work, whether language, graphics, video or coding, should consider transparently saying so.
units.fit_note: Disclosure is only to be considered, and the audience is employees rather than students submitting work.

units.why: The advisory says transparency 'may also encourage others to give AI tools a try'; this is a benefit claim about AI adoption, P87, informs.
units.anchor: Your transparency may also encourage others to give AI tools a try.
units.fit_note: Closest to a stated benefit; it is really a rationale for disclosure.

units.why: 'Do Not Conceal AI Use from colleagues, students or others' bans hiding AI use; it is a disclosure rule, P28 (nondisclosure as the violation), must-not, and it reaches students as audience.
units.anchor: Do Not Conceal AI Use
units.policy: Do not conceal AI use from colleagues, students or others.
units.fit_note: Concealment is barred as a rule for employees; no consequence is stated.

units.why: AI note-taking should be disclosed in the same way people are told a Teams or Zoom meeting is recorded, 'we should be transparent if we have an AI taking notes'; this is consent or notice for AI recording, P86.
units.anchor: we should be transparent if we have an AI taking notes.
units.fit_note: It asks for notice, not explicit permission, before AI note-taking.

units.why: Notes made by AI 'can make mistakes or misunderstand different accents' and must be reviewed for accuracy; this is verify output, P31.
units.anchor: It is important to review these notes for accuracy.

units.why: Managers choosing tools should understand whether and how vendors use GenAI and how UTA data is secured, and use the Technology Acquisition Helper; this is review of vendors and tools, P65.
units.anchor: it’s important you understand if or how your vendors are using GenAI.
units.policy: Staff who manage the selection or use of tools understand if or how their vendors are using GenAI and, when selecting new solutions, use UTA's Technology Acquisition Helper.

units.why: The page lists 'AI Feature Certification Policy (WIP)', signaling that a policy is under development; it states the policy is provisional, P54.
units.anchor: AI Feature Certification Policy (WIP)
units.policy: UTA lists an AI Feature Certification Policy that is a work in progress.
units.fit_note: Shows a policy in development, not an explicit commitment to revisit.

documents.unit: Center for Research on Teaching and Learning Excellence (CRTLE)
documents.title: Getting Started with AI and Teaching
documents.summary: A faculty-facing hub that points to UTA's required syllabus AI statement, its campus guidelines for instruction and a list of blog posts and workshops. It says AI use may be restricted, guided or integrated by instructor and gives a checklist for stating expectations.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'UTA supports faculty choice: AI use may be restricted, guided, or integrated depending on disciplinary context and course goals', so it sets no stance and leaves the decision to instructors.

units.why: The page opens as support for faculty beginning to explore AI, 'beginner-friendly and low-pressure'; it is faculty support for learning AI, P63.
units.anchor: intentionally designed to be beginner‑friendly and low‑pressure
units.policy: The page is designed for UTA faculty who are beginning to explore AI in teaching and learning to be beginner-friendly and low-pressure.

units.why: Foundational ideas state that generative AI systems 'do not think, reason, or understand in human ways'; this defines what AI is and is not, P61.
units.anchor: they do not think, reason, or understand in human ways

units.why: 'Effective teaching with AI begins with pedagogy and learning goals, not with tools' ties AI decisions to learning goals, P83.
units.anchor: begins with pedagogy and learning goals, not with tools

units.why: 'UTA supports faculty choice: AI use may be restricted, guided, or integrated' leaves the course decision to faculty and names three modes; the main code is P04 (instructor sets the rule). P05 is not chosen as the sentence names categories only loosely and gives no defined tiers.
units.anchor: UTA supports faculty choice: AI use may be restricted, guided, or integrated

units.why: The guidelines are 'campus-approved' and 'outline how faculty can make transparent, ethical decisions'; they address integrity, accessibility, privacy and communication and are the starting point for aligning with expectations; P56 as an institution-wide framework.
units.anchor: This campus‑approved guidance outlines how faculty can make transparent, ethical decisions about AI use.

units.why: The page names UTA's guidance as 'an essential starting point for aligning AI use with UTA expectations'; it tells faculty to align with guidance, which is P78-like but for faculty; the closest is P56.
units.anchor: an essential starting point for aligning AI use with UTA expectations
units.fit_note: The unit is an instruction to faculty to align with campus guidance, which the type does not capture.

units.why: UTA faculty authored an open educational resource with 'practical, classroom-ready activities' for integrating AI into teaching; this is support for faculty in learning AI, P63.
units.anchor: practical, classroom‑ready activities and examples for integrating AI into teaching

units.why: Institute materials introduce prompt design, authenticity, workforce relevance and ethical boundaries and 'emphasize experimentation over surveillance'; this describes faculty AI support, P63; the experimentation-over-surveillance stance is partly P60-like but not a statement of declining to police.
units.anchor: emphasize experimentation over surveillance
units.fit_note: It also takes a stance preferring experimentation to surveillance.

units.why: The AI Essentials Modules are 'short, faculty-focused modules' on AI capabilities and limitations; providing training for faculty is P63 (faculty-only support, not P70).
units.anchor: short, faculty‑focused modules build declarative knowledge about AI capabilities, limitations

units.why: The institute discussions show 'instructors are reframing assignments and learning outcomes rather than focusing solely on detection or restriction'; this is redesign around AI, P35.
units.anchor: reframing assignments and learning outcomes rather than focusing solely on detection or restriction

units.why: The page says CRTLE workshop materials give 'examples of syllabus language, discussion prompts, and instructional framing' for stating expectations; it offers faculty support, P63.
units.anchor: provide examples of syllabus language, discussion prompts, and instructional framing

units.why: Step 3 suggests students critique an AI-generated response to find errors or missing perspectives; this is a classroom activity that builds evaluation of AI output, nearest P31 (verify output), with a note that the unit is an instructor practice.
units.anchor: Have students critique an AI‑generated response to identify strengths, errors
units.fit_note: Shows an assignment that builds AI use into coursework, offered as a suggestion rather than a requirement.

units.why: The page suggests AI role-play or simulation tools 'to support practice-based learning'; instructors may build AI use into coursework, P79 (AI built into coursework).
units.anchor: Use AI role‑play or simulation tools to support practice‑based learning
units.fit_note: Offered as an example of a small teaching practice, not a requirement.

units.why: Instructors may 'use AI privately to draft rubrics, discussion prompts, or feedback language, then revise'; this is instructor AI use for teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: Use AI privately to draft rubrics, discussion prompts, or feedback language

units.why: The checklist item 'Clearly state whether AI use is allowed, restricted, or guided' tells instructors to state their AI position to students; this is P09 (state in the syllabus or assignment).
units.anchor: Clearly state whether AI use is allowed, restricted, or guided

units.why: The checklist asks instructors to specify acceptable uses such as brainstorming, revision and coding support; it directs how an expectations statement is made, P09; P12-P15 not chosen since the examples are only illustrations.
units.anchor: Specify what types of AI use are acceptable

units.why: The checklist asks instructors to explain what is not permitted, with the example of submitting AI-generated work 'as original without acknowledgment'; a statement of prohibited uses in the syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: Explain what is not permitted
units.fit_note: The example also signals that AI work passed off as original without acknowledgment is a misuse.

units.why: The checklist tells instructors to 'tell students how to acknowledge or cite AI assistance'; the rule is that instructors set a citation method, nearest P24 (disclose AI use), addressed to instructors.
units.anchor: Tell students how to acknowledge or cite AI assistance
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors to explain the method; it does not itself oblige students to disclose.

units.why: The page states the Quick Start crowd-sourced language 'does not replace the required AI policy statement per the syllabus statement'; it says a UTA AI policy statement in the syllabus is required, P09 (require an AI statement in every syllabus).
units.anchor: This does not replace the required AI policy statement
units.policy: A required AI policy statement appears in every UTA syllabus; crowd-sourced language does not replace it.

units.why: The page points to the Provost's UTA syllabus statements, which have AI policy options on pages 12-13; this is a university-provided set of syllabus options (tiers/options), P05, offered to faculty.
units.anchor: with AI policy options on pages 12-13
units.policy: UTA provides AI policy options for syllabus statements on pages 12-13 of its Statements to Use in Your Syllabus document.
units.fit_note: The options themselves are not in the fetched text, so the tiers are not named.

units.why: The page says 'AI tools and policies will continue to evolve' and that faculty should view AI learning as ongoing; this is a provisional-policy statement, P54.
units.anchor: AI tools and policies will continue to evolve.

units.why: The page states UTA's approach 'emphasizes faculty agency, ethical practice, and community learning'; it leaves the decision with faculty, P04.
units.anchor: emphasizes faculty agency, ethical practice, and community learning
units.fit_note: Also names ethical practice and community learning as values.

units.why: CRTLE offers 'one-on-one teaching consultations, workshops, and AI-focused resources' to help faculty refine syllabus language; this supports faculty in learning AI, P63.
units.anchor: one‑on‑one teaching consultations, workshops, and AI‑focused resources

units.why: A blog summary describes shifting 'from detecting misuse to preparing students for AI-mediated workplaces' and AI literacy as a learning outcome; this is the career-based reason to teach AI, P44.
units.anchor: preparing students for AI‑mediated workplaces

units.why: A blog recap says it focuses on 'clarity, transparency, and assignment-specific AI policies'; it endorses setting AI rules per assignment, P04.
units.anchor: clarity, transparency, and assignment‑specific AI policies

notes: Guidelines for Instruction PDF and Quick Start pages were not collected (404), so syllabus AI policy options on pages 12-13 are not coded. The first document is employee data advisory; student-facing rules are almost absent.
